pageCache.text:
Welcome
to Kenmont Primary School
I hope that you will find our website informative, useful and interesting.
We are a small friendly school which has been judged to be good by Ofsted (January 2023). Our school is popular with local families, who value the benefits that a small school offers including a close community, committed staff and an ethos that values each child. We offer a happy and friendly atmosphere and are dedicated to providing an inspiring and engaging curriculum so that children grow to their full potential and become responsible, caring members of the community.
Kenmont works closely with Brackenbury Primary School and Wendell Park Primary School within a partnership arrangement sharing an Executive Head teacher. The partnership enables our staff to work collaboratively and share expertise with other teachers for the benefit of the Kenmont children.
David Collins, Executive Head teacher

Vision & Values
Vision & Values
Our Vision
At Kenmont, our vision is for all our children to be able to reach their full potential, be ready for the next stage of their education and to be life-long learners.
The Kenmont Way nurtures confidence and happiness by experiencing a creative, broad and balanced curriculum underpinned by the Kenmont Values.
We have high expectations for all children in their academic learning, responsibility to their community and as future global citizens.
Our Values
Each month, one value is explored and celebrated with the children and the adults at our school.
The Values are part of a 2 year cycle:
1. Caring, courage, patience, friendship, hope, love, co-operation, responsibility, fairness, independence, appreciation2. Respect, happiness, peace, generosity, honesty, simplicity, trust, unity, understanding, thoughtfulness, tolerance
Through these core values we aspire for our staff and children to treat and behave towards one and other in a supportive and respectful manner.
We aspire for all our pupils achieving to the best of their ability in a school community with high expectations. We value learning and community above all else.
At Kenmont we follow a values based education exploring and celebrating a different value each month.

SMSC & British Values
SMSC & British Values
Spiritual, Moral, Social and Cultural (SMSC) Provision
At Kenmont Primary School, spiritual, moral, social and cultural education underpin all aspects of school life. This work is absolutely integral to everything we do. It plays a significant role in contributing to the high levels of motivation, tolerance and excellent that the children demonstrate at our school.
The individuality of each child is valued and respected in order that:
This is not a “subject” in itself but opportunities to promote it are actively planned for across all subject areas of the curriculum; within collective worship; within our behaviour policy, within our safeguarding policy and within everything we do. It has particularly strong links to our work in Personal, Social and Health Education and Religious Education.
Definitions of terms
Spiritual development is the growth of insights, beliefs, attitudes and values which guide and motivate us. Through spiritual development, children can gain a sense of identity, their own self-worth and broader meaning and purpose in life.
Moral development is the building of a framework of moral values which control our personal behaviour. There is a recognition within this area of development that in a multi-racial, multicultural and multi-faith democracy such as Britain there will always be debate about moral values and these will differ from person to person.
Social development is concerned with the each child’s ability to develop the skills, understanding and personal qualities necessary for living and functioning effectively in our multi-racial, multicultural and multi-faith society and to be able to contribute to that society.
Cultural development is the about helping children to understand their own cultural heritage alongside the cultural traditions of the school, the local community, those of the wider British community and the wider world. They will explore these different cultures in order that they are able to understand, accept, respect and celebrate the differences and similarities they discover.
British Values
The DfE have reinforced the need “To create and enforce a clear and rigorous expectation on all schools to promote the fundamental British values of democracy, the rule of law, individual liberty and mutual respect and tolerance of those with different faiths and beliefs.”
Kenmont Primary School is committed to serving its community and surrounding areas. It recognises the multi-cultural, multi-faith and ever-changing nature of the United Kingdom, and therefore those it serves. It also understands the vital role it has in ensuring that groups or individuals within the school are not subjected to intimidation or radicalisation by those wishing to unduly, or illegally, influence them.
Our school, accepts admissions from all those entitled to an education under British law. It follows the policies outlined by the governing body regarding equal opportunities, which guarantee that there will be no discrimination against any individual or group, regardless of faith, ethnicity, gender, sexuality, political or financial status, or similar.
The Government emphasises that schools are required to ensure that key ‘British Values’ are taught in all UK schools. The government set out its definition of British values in the departmental advice entitled ‘Promoting Fundamental British Values as part of SMSC’ – DfE November 2014 which links to the ‘Prevent Duty’ – DfE June 2015 that requires all schools to have “due regard to the need to prevent people from being drawn into terrorism”.
The fundamental British Values that schools should have regard to are those of:
Democracy
The rule of law
Individual liberty
Mutual respect

Executive Head's Welcome
Executive Head’s Welcome
Welcome to Kenmont Primary School
I hope that you will find our website informative, useful and interesting.
We are a small friendly school which has been judged to be good by Ofsted (January 2023). Our school is popular with local families, who value the benefits that a small school offers including a close community, committed staff and an ethos that values each child. We offer a happy and friendly atmosphere and are dedicated to providing an inspiring and engaging curriculum so that children grow to their full potential and become responsible, caring members of the community.
Kenmont works closely with Brackenbury Primary School and Wendell Park Primary School within a Federation sharing an Executive Head teacher. The federation enables our staff to work collaboratively and share expertise with other teachers for the benefit of the Kenmont children.
Executive Head teacher, Brackenbury, Kenmont and Wendell Park Federation.

School Federation
School Federation
The Federation– Brackenbury, Kenmont and Wendell Park Primary School Federation
Kenmont is a member of the Brackenbury, Kenmont and Wendell Park Primary School Federation. Since September 2014, Kenmont and Wendell Park Primary schools have operated with a shared Executive Head teacher. In September 2021, the partnership expanded with Brackenbury Primary School joining. The Federation is led by Executive Head teacher, Dave Collins. In April 2023 the informal partnership changed to a Federation.
Each of the schools is a LA maintained community school and each school has it’s own unique identity. We aspire for our schools to be the number one choice for their local community, because they provide a broad, engaging and fun education.
The shared aims of our federation are:
Working closely together with the Executive Head teacher, the schools benefit from: distributed leadership model, strong subject leadership, a rigorous cycle of innovation and staff development, and a community committed to our shared values.
to strengthen each school by working collaboratively,
to strengthen accountability within each school,
to empower the leaders of each school.

Personal Development and Enrichment
Personal Development & Enrichment
What is Personal Development
Personal Development (PD) is the planned provision that enables pupils to develop the knowledge, skills, values and behaviours they need to thrive both now and in later life. It prepares pupils for adulthood by promoting character, resilience, wellbeing, healthy relationships, active citizenship and an understanding of the diverse society in which they live.
Personal Development should equip pupils with the knowledge, skills, attitudes and values they need to stay safe, build positive relationships, manage their physical and mental wellbeing, make informed and responsible decisions, and participate confidently and respectfully in school and society. Through high-quality Personal, Social and Health Education (PSHE), Relationships and Health Education (RHE), the wider curriculum and enrichment opportunities pupils are prepared for the responsibilities, opportunities and experiences of later life.
Enrichment should provide all pupils with equitable access to a wide range of meaningful experiences beyond the taught curriculum that broaden horizons, develop skills, raise aspirations, strengthen wellbeing and belonging, and prepare them for successful participation in society and adult life. This includes developing a solid understanding of fundamental British Values.
Vision
We believe that education extends far beyond the acquisition of academic knowledge. Every child deserves a rich, ambitious education that nurtures the whole person and enables them to flourish academically, socially, emotionally, physically and morally. Through a carefully planned programme of personal development and enrichment, we ensure that every pupil is equipped with the knowledge, skills, experiences and character needed to thrive in modern Britain and contribute positively to society.
Our Personal Development Curriculum reflects our commitment to providing an equitable entitlement for every child. We recognise that pupils arrive at school with differing experiences and opportunities; therefore, our curriculum is deliberately designed to broaden horizons, raise aspirations and remove barriers to participation. Every pupil, regardless of background or circumstance, is entitled to high-quality enrichment that develops confidence, resilience, creativity, leadership and a lifelong love of learning.
Personal development is not viewed as an 'add-on' to our curriculum. It is woven throughout school life, enriching learning within the classroom and beyond it. Through meaningful experiences, positive relationships and purposeful opportunities to contribute, pupils develop the confidence to make informed choices, appreciate diversity, care for others and become active citizens within their local, national and global communities.
By the time pupils leave our school, they will have experienced a broad and balanced programme of enrichment that enables them to:
understand themselves and their place within society
appreciate and celebrate diversity
develop resilience and independence
develop leadership and teamwork skills
Curriculum Intent
We aim to provide a coherent and progressive curriculum that:
Our curriculum is underpinned by the Department for Education's Enrichment Framework and complements our academic curriculum, Relationships and Health Education (RHE), Physical Education, Religious Education, Computing and wider pastoral provision.
develops confident, articulate and resilient learners
promotes kindness, respect, empathy and inclusion
encourages curiosity about the wider world
fosters healthy lifestyles and positive wellbeing
promotes environmental stewardship and sustainability
provides meaningful opportunities for leadership and service
broadens aspirations through memorable experiences and encounters.
The Purpose of Personal Development
Personal development enables children to become the very best version of themselves.
We believe that pupils need more than excellent academic outcomes. They also need opportunities to develop confidence, resilience, independence, compassion and ambition through meaningful experiences that challenge and inspire them.
Our curriculum therefore provides a carefully sequenced progression of experiences that enable pupils to:
Every enrichment opportunity has been carefully selected because it contributes towards these long-term outcomes.
develop positive relationships
understand rights and responsibilities
make informed decisions
contribute to their communities
appreciate creativity and culture
enjoy healthy and active lifestyles
develop practical life skills
become responsible global citizens.
Key Areas of the Personal Development Curriculum:
Relationships - Healthy respectful relationships are key to a happy and safe existence.
Development of character - It is key that pupils have the opportunity to explore and express their character and build the skills they need for resilience, empathy and employability.
Citizenship - It is crucial for pupils to develop key knowledge, skills and understanding to prepare them to play a full and active part in society. In particular, build their awareness and understanding of democracy, government and how laws are made and upheld.
British values (BV) - The DfE states that all schools need to promote the fundamental British values of: Democracy, Respect for the rule of law, Individual liberty, Mutual respect, Tolerance of those of different faiths and beliefs. Teaching BV supports the government aim to create a more cohesive and integrated society, as well a way to protect children from extremist ideologies.
Physical and mental health education - Physical and mental well-being are equally important in helping pupils to maintain a healthy life style.
Wider opportunities - Enrichment experiences (extra –curricular and curricular) are key components for ensuring a high quality PD provision. The school exposes pupils to a range of wider opportunities that broaden their horizons and facilitates them to discover their true talents and interests. We have a list of experiences we want every child to have experienced before they leave primary school.
Social, Moral, Spiritual and Cultural (SMSC) development
Essentially, SMSC is about helping students develop a range of personal and social skills that will enable them to become well-rounded, responsible, and engaged members of society.
Spiritual development: Pupils learn about insights, beliefs, attitudes and values which guide and motivate us. They develop a sense of identity, their own self-worth and broader meaning and purpose in life.
Moral development: Pupils build awareness and understanding of moral values which control our personal behaviour. They recognise that in a multi-racial, multicultural and multi-faith democracy such as Britain there will always be debate about moral values and these will differ from person to person.
Social development: Pupils develop the ability develop the skills, understanding and personal qualities necessary for living and functioning effectively in our multi-racial, multicultural and multi-faith society and to be able to contribute to that society.
Cultural development: Pupils build understanding their own cultural heritage alongside the cultural traditions of the school, the local community, those of the wider British community and the wider world. They will explore these different cultures in order that they are able to understand, accept, respect and celebrate the differences and similarities they discover.
Spotting and honing exceptional talent
As a school we committed to identifying those pupils who exhibit exceptional talents or gifts in specific areas. We hone pupils’ talents by offering further opportunities beyond the classroom. This is accomplished through the use of external agencies and experts, who are able to develop the skills of our pupils to a standard that is beyond the expectation of the primary curriculum. This includes scholarships, working in partnership with established organisations and offering pupils the opportunity to showcase their talents to wider audiences. We strongly believe that this approach enables pupils to flourish. We also recognise the impact of this as it could be, for some pupils, the catalyst for a lifelong career.
Personal development across school life
Personal development is delivered through a wide range of experiences, including:
Together, these experiences provide every pupil with a coherent, ambitious and memorable journey through primary education.
the taught curriculum
assemblies
themed enrichment weeks
educational visits
residential experiences
extra-curricular clubs
pupil leadership opportunities
sporting competitions
performances
community partnerships
outdoor learning
charitable initiatives
celebration events
pupil voice activities.
The Experiences Guarantee
We believe that memorable experiences are central to children's personal development. We therefore guarantee that every pupil will have access to a carefully planned entitlement of enrichment experiences throughout their primary education.
These experiences are not isolated events. They are deliberately sequenced to deepen children's knowledge, confidence and independence over time.
The full entitlement is detailed later in this document but every child will, before leaving Year 6:
perform to an audience
visit theatres, museums and galleries
participate in competitive sport
contribute to charitable or community projects
take on positions of responsibility
learn about democracy and citizenship
experience enterprise and financial education
engage with STEM learning beyond the classroom
participate in cultural celebrations
visit places of worship
develop environmental awareness through sustainability projects
prepare confidently for secondary education.
The Five Enrichment Strands
Our Personal Development Curriculum is organised around the five strands identified within the Department for Education's Enrichment Framework.
Developing responsible citizens who contribute positively to society.
Developing creativity, cultural understanding and appreciation of the arts.
Nature, Outdoors and Adventure
Building resilience, environmental stewardship and a lifelong connection with nature.
Sport and Physical Activity
Promoting healthy lifestyles, teamwork, perseverance and enjoyment of physical activity.
Developing Wider Life and Future Skills
Equipping pupils with practical knowledge, digital confidence and the skills needed for future success.
Each strand is planned as a progressive curriculum from Nursery to Year 6, ensuring pupils revisit key concepts while developing increasing independence, responsibility and leadership.
Civic Engagement
We believe that every child has the potential to make a positive contribution to their school, their local community and the wider world.
Our Civic Engagement curriculum develops pupils' understanding of democracy, responsibility, fairness, equality and active citizenship. Through meaningful opportunities to contribute, pupils learn that their voices matter and that they have the power to bring about positive change.
Beginning with a strong sense of belonging in Nursery and Reception, pupils progressively develop the confidence, knowledge and leadership skills needed to participate actively in school life, represent the views of others and contribute to their community.
By the end of Year 6, pupils understand that good citizens demonstrate kindness, integrity, responsibility and service. They leave ready to participate positively in British society and to contribute confidently to their future communities.

Governing Board
Brackenbury, Kenmont & Wendell Park Federaton Governing Board
We want to take this opportunity to introduce ourselves and the role we play at each school.
The Governing Board has an important part to play in raising school standards. We set the strategic direction for the schools, ensure financial accountability and monitor and evaluate school performance. While the Executive Head teacher and Heads of School are responsible for the day-to-day running of each school, our role is often described as acting as “a critical friend”. We provide strategic governance to ensure that all children get the best possible education, constantly challenging the schools to attain the best possible performance.
We have responsibility together with the leadership teams for agreeing the policies for the general running of each school. We fulfil statutory duties to ensure that each school is a safe, healthy and inclusive environment. We provide support and challenge to the leadership team of each school on all issues that affect the learning and welfare of our pupils. We also have a responsibility to handle complaints, though it is important to note that individual problems should, at the outset, be directed first to your child’s teacher and then to the school’s leadership team.
The governing Board is drawn from the school staff, parents of children at the schools, the community that our schools serve and people who have applied through – or been nominated by – the Local Authority. The usual term of office is four years but many governors stand for re-election and serve more than one term.
If you are interested in the work we do, would like to find out more, have any questions – or are interested in becoming a governor, please contact the school.
The full Governing Board meets once a term, and there are sub-committees dealing with Resources & Finance and Curriculum & Standards. Once approved, the Minutes of all our meetings are available from any school office.
Governing Board Membership and Appointing Bodies
The current and historical membership of the Governing Board can be viewed online at each schools 'Get Information About Schools' webpage which lists each governor's terms of office and appointing body. Pen Portraits of our current board can also be viewed at the bottom of this page. Brackenbury - Get Information About SchoolsKenmont - Get Information About SchoolsWendell Park Get Information About Schools
Governing Board Diversity Information
Diversity is important and the DfE want governing boards to be increasingly reflective of the communities they serve.
The DfE encourages schools to collect and publish governing board members’ diversity data. Board members can opt out of sharing their information, including protected characteristics, at any given time and so the information below may not include all members of the board.

Governor Pen Portraits
Please click on each photo to see a short biography of each governor.
Ms Wendi Webber
I have lived in Hammersmith and Fulham for 30+ years and I have been a governor for 17 years and a Chair of Governor's for 12 years. Both of my children attended Kenmont Primary School.
I am a professional musician and music teacher. I teach in the state and private sectors and I am passionate about making sure that our children in the state sector get as many opportunities and have as good outcomes as children in the private sector.
During the past few years I have seen the benefits of working in partnership with other schools and I am excited to see the further developments to come across each of the three schools in the federation .
Ms Anna Armstrong
Anna is an Assistant Head, (Higher Education and Careers) at Godolphin and Latymer School in Hammersmith where she has worked for over a decade.
Prior to becoming an Assistant Head, Anna has been the Head of History and Politics at both G&L and the John Lyon School in Harrow.
Anna studied for a BA Honours in History at the University of York before completing her PGCE at UCL IOE. She has undertaken UCL's Senior Leadership qualification and is a member of the Careers Development Institute.
Mandy Byrne
A resident of West London since university, I worked in primary education as a teacher, SENCo and Deputy Headteacher in the borough of Westminster for 27 years and moved to St Mary's University, Twickenham 10 years ago as a senior lecturer in primary education training teachers.
I have been a co-opted governor for a special needs specialist school as well as a staff governor in a mainstream primary school.
I am committed to the wellbeing and progress of all children with a particular interest in the support and development of children with special educational needs. I have trained as a dyslexia specialist teacher and a person-centred trainer focusing on the needs of individual children and working closely with their families.
Ms Alice Careless
Born and brought up in the local area, I was a pupil of Brackenbury in the 1980s. Both of my children have attended the school with my youngest moving on in July 2021. I joined as a parent governor in 2015 and was most recently the co-chair of governors at Brackenbury. I am a Co-opted governor. I have spent the last 24 years working in a number of local government and charitable organisations providing advice and advocacy for the local community. I am currently working for a national charity providing welfare advice, financial assistance and wellbeing support. ‹
Ms Ffion Cartwright
I've lived in Hammersmith and Fulham for the past three years and it's a place I'm proud to call home. I currently work as a Strategy Advisor in the Secretary of State for Housing, Policy and Strategy Unit, where I help drive forward long-term policy across government. My experience in public service-as well as my role as a proud aunty to two nieces- has given me a strong appreciation for the role that education plays in building confidence, nurturing potential and breaking down barriers to opportunity.
As one of the newest members of the governing board, I've thoroughly enjoyed getting to know the school, its staff, and the wider community. I'm excited to contribute to its continued success and support its strategic development in the years ahead.
Mr David Collins
I have been the head teacher at Brackenbury since September 2016 and Executive Head since September 2021. Prior to that I was a Head teacher of a primary school in Hampshire. I started my teaching career in 2001 in Hampshire and have taught and worked in a variety of Primary and Junior Schools. I enjoy working with governors in setting the strategic direction of the school and celebrating the schools achievements.
Ms Gilly Di Loreto
I've proudly called Hammersmith and Fulham home for nearly three decades, and my two sons are currently thriving at Wendell Park Primary School. In my day-to-day life, I work in the healthcare sector, where I help manage various services and provide support to those in need.
I'm genuinely eager to delve into the inner workings of our schools, discover how we can assist parents, and understand the steps we can take to support the growth and well-being of our children.
Paige Dwyer
I have been teaching for 9 years and feel proud to be part of the Kenmont community. Over the past three years, I've worked across the Brackenbury, Wendell, and Kenmont Federation, gaining valuable experience in a range of roles including Maths Lead, PSHE Lead, Phase Leader, and Writing Lead.

Curriculum
Curriculum
At Kenmont Primary School we believe each child benefits from a broad and rich curriculum.
Curriculum Intent
At Kenmont, our aim is for every child to love learning, feel confident and achieve their very best. Through a broad and rich curriculum pupils attain the knowledge that prepares them for secondary school and beyond. Pupils also develop an understanding of the world around them and the contributions they can make as citizens; and the opportunities that address any possible socioeconomic inequalities that some may face.
We have established a Curriculum which is:
Balanced: Adaptions to the curriculum to allow more time for even more important elements and foundational skills and fundamental aspects to be focused on.
Coherent: Connections are made explicit between different aspects of the curriculum; especially in reading.
Progressive: Learning builds from prior knowledge through carefully planned sequences.
Memorable: Retrieval practice to ensure learning helps pupils to retain knowledge over time.
Focused: Teachers focus on the ‘Core Knowledge’ – the most important ideas in a subject.
Relevant: Teaching ideas in a way that is engaging, interesting and motivating for pupils.
Inclusive: All children have access to the curriculum.
Our curriculum is coherently planned and sequenced to ensure progression and depth in each subject so that learners will accumulate the knowledge needed for future learning.

Foundational Skills
The Department for Education’sStrong Foundations in the First Years of Schoolguidance highlights the importance of giving children the essential knowledge, language, behaviours and learning habits they need to thrive both in school and beyond. At our school, we carefully plan opportunities for children in the Early Years and Year 1 to develop these foundational skills through high-quality teaching, purposeful play, structured routines and rich language experiences. These skills include oracy, early reading and writing, number understanding, physical development (fine and gross motor skills), independence, attention and listening, social interaction and emotional regulation. By building these strong foundations from the very beginning, we help children become confident, capable and successful learners who are well prepared for the next stages of their education.

Assessment
Assessment
The DFE has published a set of core assessment principles to help schools prepare to implement new assessment arrangements for tracking pupil progress against the new National Curriculum. The document reminds schools that there will be no national system for doing this, but that schools will be expected to demonstrate (with evidence) their assessment of pupils’ progress so that they can keep parents informed, enable governors to make judgments about the school’s effectiveness and to inform inspections by Ofsted. The document states that ‘effective assessment systems’ should:
At Kenmont, we have developed a system that builds on best practice nationally. Using a combination of exemplars, portfolios, pupil interviews and regular observations, our teachers carefully assess the needs of each child on a continuous basis.
Aims and objectives of assessment
Age-Related Expectations
The school curriculum, and expectations set in teaching and learning are focussed around Age-Related Expectations (ARE). These are the skills, knowledge and understanding children are expected to have at the end of each year group. They assess how children demonstrate, contextualise, and link these skills and understanding.
In years 1-6 assessments focus on the attainment of children against ARE. Children are, unless working below the year group expectations, tracked against key objectives in reading, writing and maths. Entry level is ‘emerging’ (E), ‘Developing’ (D) and ‘Secure’ (S). Children working above ARE are assessed as ‘Mastery’ (M).
Ongoing assessments throughout the year track individual children’s attainment in relation to the ARE for their year group and to plan the next steps in their learning.
ARE assessments in relation to the National Curriculum follow on from assessment in the Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS) where children’s attainment is assessed in relation to the 17 early learning goals (ELGs).
Children with special educational needs (SEN) should work at ARE in curriculum areas not affected by their particular needs. Children’s educational health care plans and other school interventions should enable these children to meet their personalised objectives and targets.
Assessment of learning
Informal assessment is an ongoing process and an integral part of teaching and learning in the classroom. Assessment opportunities are recorded on the planning sheets and marking reflects assessments of progress.
Formal termly assessments are made in:
One the basis of the assessments in these areas, teachers will determine whether a pupil is emerging, developing or securing the ARE. This is recorded each term.
Children in Nursery and Reception are assessed against the age-related bands for each core area of learning and development plus:
literacy
mathematics
understanding the world
expressive arts and design
Statutory Testing and Reporting
In Year 1, all children undergo ‘Phonics Screening’ to check that their phonics knowledge and skill is at, or above, a nationally expected standard. The outcomes of this screening are communicated with parents of children in Year 1. If a child fails to meet the nationally expected phonics standard, they undergo the screening again in Year 2 where there is an expectation that children will meet the standard. This reported to the parents of those children.
In Year 4, children complete the Multiplication Table Check in June. The outcomes of this assessment are shared with parents in pupils’ the end of year reports.
In Year 6, children are tested in Reading, Mathematics and Spelling Grammar and Punctuation (SPAG). End of Year 6 testing takes place for all children nationally in May. End of key stage outcomes are published using Scaled Scores. Scaled scores involve a national standard of 100. A child’s raw test score is converted into a scaled score and a child who achieves a scaled score of 100 will have met the expected national standard. Writing is teacher assessed and teachers have to submit that children are either working at the ARE in Writing, or that they are working above or below ARE. This also applies for Science.

Online Safety
Cyber bullying, grooming, violent and inappropriate images or video and sharing personal information and photos are all an online threat to children.
It is important to protect your children using the available free settings on your home devices and computers.
At Brackenbury, Kenmont and Wendell Park Federation we are committed to the use of computer technologies and recognise the internet as a valuable tool for learners of all ages. However, we acknowledge the potential for inappropriate use and access to undesirable material and thus we have a duty of care to protect our pupils through the provision of a thorough and comprehensive e-safety education.
All pupils use computer facilities, including the internet as an essential part of the curriculum and to support learning opportunities wherever possible.
Further advice - LGFL Parent Safe Website
